newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Oil-rich Nigeria has no answer to fuel scarcity.
newsitem.headline: Oil-rich Nigeria has no answer to fuel scarcity.

text.p: The fuel shortage which has gripped Nigeria for more than a month showed no sign of easing on Friday, a bitter irony in Africa's leading crude oil producer.
"From what we can see the government has no answer to this problem," said estate agent Dipo Ajayi, who had slept overnight in a petrol queue in Lagos.

The leading independent daily newspaper, The Guardian, on Friday called the fuel shortage "The Great Energy Crisis" as military ruler General Sani Abacha's ministers continued a slanging match over the crisis.

"Despite the huge amount allocated for the repairs of the refineries, we have found that these have not been repaired, the result of which is persistent shortage of fuel in Nigeria, the world's sixth largest producer of crude oil," finance minister Anthony Ani said in a public lecture last weekend.
He said $440 million and $295 million were allocated to Nigerian National Petroleum Corporation (NNPC) in 1995 and 1996 respectively for projects including refinery repairs.

But oil minister Dan Etete disputed this in a statement on Thursday night in which he called Ani's remarks "a deliberate falsehood with intent to incite the Nigerian masses and pitch the international community against not only the Ministry of Petroleum Resources and the NNPC but to embarrass and discredit the present administration."
Nigeria has four oil refineries but suffers recurrent fuel shortages, with the current one crippling Lagos, the nation's commercial hub, stranding commuters and hitting businesses.
"To come to work today was not easy," said Chris Diala, a driver who lives in the suburbs and works in the city centre. "We are spending all our income on transport."
Etete said, "Government is aware of the present fuel situation and while regretting the inconveniences to the public, is addressing the matter with a view to finding a lasting solution."
Nigeria's four refineries have a combined capacity of 445,000 barrels of crude oil daily but produce at only a fraction of their capacity due to deteriorating facilities.

"We are a laughing stock throughout the world because 'oil-rich' Nigeria can't deliver ordinary petrol to its citizens," a spokesman for the Civil Liberties Organisation, the leading human rights group, said.

Long queues have become a common feature at petrol stations and a black market is booming with people paying as much 4,000 naira ($47) for a 50-litre can of petrol, more than seven times the normal price.
So far no official explanation of the exact cause of the shortage has been given.

Government officials have offered contradictory explanations for the scarcity, including ageing refineries, non-compliance with refinery maintenance schedules and non-disbursement of budgeted funds for the refineries by the federal authorities.
Some have called for imports but say this is unlikely because of a ban by Abacha on imports since September last year.
Nigeria, a major player in the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC), produces roughly two million barrels a day (bpd) of crude oil.
Of this, 250,000 bpd is allocated to the four refineries with a combined capacity to process 445,000 bpd of crude. --Lagos newsroom +234 1 2630317 ($ = 84.4 Nigerian Naira)
